intro: Santa Cruz's big redwoods are in Felton, about ten kilometres north of town, on the short Redwood Grove loop in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park. Stop 7 is The Giant, 270 feet tall and over 17 feet wide by the park's own guide. Stop 8 is the Fremont Tree, a burnt-out, still-living redwood you can step inside, where a general may or may not have spent a night in 1846. He refused to confirm it. The walk is flat, and a day-use fee applies.
meta_description: The Giant and the hollow Fremont Tree, two old-growth coast redwoods on the Redwood Grove loop at Henry Cowell park in Felton, near Santa Cruz.
question_meta: The oldest tree we map near Santa Cruz is likely The Giant, a Felton coast redwood; estimates of 1,200 to 1,800 years are a hedge.
question_answer: The oldest tree we map near Santa Cruz is probably The Giant, a Coast Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) at stop 7 of the Redwood Grove loop in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, Felton. A roughly 1,500-year figure comes from a visitor's caption, and nothing official dates this trunk; 1,200 to 1,800 years is a hedge.
question_context: California State Parks gives The Giant two numbers in its trail guide, 270 feet tall and more than 17 feet wide, and leaves its age alone. The guide's only remark on age is general, that a mature redwood can pass 2,000 years. A visitor's dated photograph from 2026 is captioned at roughly 1,500 years and about 277 feet. A figure of 1,200 to 1,600 years has also been attributed to State Parks for the park's tallest redwood, but we have not seen the original. The next stop on the loop is the Fremont Tree, burnt out and hollow and still alive, with a base you can step into. General John C. Fremont reportedly slept in it in 1846, and when he was asked about that in 1888, his reply was that it made a great story and should stand. The grove was Santa Cruz County Big Trees Park before it became a state park in 1953, after the Cowell family gave the land. Felton is about ten kilometres north of Santa Cruz, the loop is short and flat, and the park charges a day-use fee.

faq.q: How tall is The Giant at Henry Cowell?
faq.a: The State Parks trail guide gives 270 feet, with a trunk more than 17 feet wide. A visitor's caption from 2026 says about 277 feet.

faq.q: Did Fremont really sleep in the Fremont Tree?
faq.a: He reportedly did in 1846. Asked in 1888, he said it makes a great story and to let it stand, which is not a yes.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see these redwoods?
faq.a: Yes, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park charges a day-use fee. Check parks.ca.gov for current hours.

trees.story:
The Giant is 270 feet tall and more than 17 feet wide, and that is roughly all anyone official will say about it. Those two figures come from the California State Parks guide to the Redwood Grove loop, where it is stop 7. It stands in Felton, about 10 kilometres north of Santa Cruz.

Its age is a harder question. A visitor's caption on a dated 2026 photograph says roughly 1,500 years and about 277 feet. The park guide offers only the general remark that a mature redwood can pass 2,000 years. A figure of 1,200 to 1,600 years has been attributed to State Parks for the tallest redwood in the park, though we have not seen the original. So a range of 1,200 to 1,800 is a hedge, and nobody we have found has dated this trunk.

The grove was Santa Cruz County Big Trees Park before the Cowell family's land gift made it a state park in 1953.

The loop is short and flat, and the hollow Fremont Tree is the very next stop. There is a day-use fee.

trees.name: The Fremont Tree

location.address: Redwood Grove Loop Trail, stop 8, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, Felton, Santa Cruz County
location.neighbourhood: Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, Felton

trees.story:
General John C. Fremont was asked in 1888 whether he had really slept inside this redwood, and he declined to spoil it. "It makes a great story, let it stand," he said, according to the California State Parks guide to the Redwood Grove loop. So the claim that he spent a night here in 1846 remains exactly that, a good claim its own subject refused to confirm.

The tree does not need him. Fire hollowed out the base and it went on living. The park describes it as a still-living tree and invites you to explore the inside, so you can stand in the room that may or may not have housed a general. Dated observations from 2022, 2025 and 2026 show it still here.

No girth, height or age has been published for it. It is simply an old-growth redwood with a burnt heart and a better publicist than most. If you know its age, tell us.

It is stop 8 on the loop, in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park at Felton, right after The Giant. There is a state park day-use fee.
